kandidaty.zagolovok: A practical guide to shipping with Claude Code
kandidaty.tekst: After you open a pull request, hand the follow up to Claude Code using /ship. Here's how to dial in your preferences to stay in flow.

- Added skills from MCP servers (beta). They show as server:skill in the / menu; other skills keep their names
- Added a PreSkillShellCommand hook event that can refuse a skill or command's inline shell commands as it loads; on 2.1.331 and older, a settings file naming it opens a dialog at start
- Added "Always deliver" to the prompt for held messages from other sessions
- Added a footer line that stays while a flagged message has your session on a different model, until you pick one with /model
- Added an OpenTelemetry assistant_response event for text Claude sends through SendUserMessage or Cowork's message tool, when response logging is on
- Added a warning in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when part of a session couldn't be saved, saying how to save it with /compact
- Added a notice in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when a resumed session's earlier messages weren't loaded, as the terminal already shows
- Added your Cyber Verification Program access tier to the startup header, beside the model name when your tier applies to that model and you're signed in with a claude.ai account
- [VSCode] Added a notification in more cases when closing a proposed diff leaves the edit unapplied, and stopped the diff notifications on a split copy of an answered diff
- [VSCode] Added a warning when restoring a conversation with /rewind in the side bar stops a self-paced /loop
- [VSCode] Added the installed version to the rows of Manage plugins
- Updated computer use on macOS to newer safety rules, so some actions are refused and typing can be slower
- Changed terminal and VS Code sessions moved to Sonnet 5 or 5.5 on Bedrock Mantle, Agent Platform and Foundry to start in auto mode if no mode is set; set disableAutoMode to "disable" to stop it
- Changed the sonnet model alias on Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry to Sonnet 5.5, and Foundry's opus alias to Opus 5.5; sonnet on Amazon Bedrock stays at Sonnet 4.5
- Changed the default model on Microsoft Foundry to Sonnet 5.5: deploy claude-sonnet-5-5, or set ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL to a model you have deployed
- Changed sonnet and background requests on Google Cloud's Agent Platform to read VERTEX_REGION_CLAUDE_5_5_SONNET; with only the 4_5 variable set they go to CLOUD_ML_REGION or us-east5
- Changed --model default and a Default pick to move to an older model when that model isn't available, instead of stopping with an error; in auto mode, only to a model auto mode accepts
- Changed Microsoft Foundry: Claude Sonnet 4, Opus 4 and Opus 4.1 now count as retired, so step-downs stop above them and a pin to one warns that it was retired
- Changed the Claude apps gateway's built-in model list: Sonnet 5.5 replaces Sonnet 4.5 as its second model, and Claude Desktop starts on it where a policy allows no Opus 4.6
- Changed SDK and claude -p mid-turn messages to count as the user's where feature flags aren't fetched, as on clouds or with telemetry off, from Opus 4.8 on; mark relayed text isSynthetic: tr

kandidaty.tekst:
- A fix is live for an undercount of web searches in the List User Activity endpoint of the Claude Enterprise Analytics API. kandidaty.zagolovok: Claude Platform release notes — November 23, 2026
kandidaty.tekst:

kandidaty.zagolovok: Claude Platform release notes — November 23, 2026
kandidaty.tekst:
- On November 24, 2026, a fix for an undercount of project activity in the Claude Enterprise Analytics API will go live. The Get Chat Project Usage endpoint leaves out some messages in project chats. One example is messages sent after a chat moves into a Cowork cloud session. After the fix, it will count most of those messages. message_count, distinct_conversation_count, and distinct_user_count can then be higher, and more projects can appear in the results.

- The List User Activity endpoint will change in the same way when you filter by project_id. message_count and distinct_conversation_count can be higher, last_activity_date can be later, and more users can appear. Without the filter, some of these messages count in chat_cowork_unified_metrics.sessions.message_count. So the chat message_count for a user can be higher with the filter than without it.

- The project fix will apply to data for November 20, 2026 (UTC), and later, so counts that you already pulled for those days can change. It does not recount earlier days.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
kandidaty.tekst:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enable

kandidaty.zagolovok: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
kandidaty.tekst:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, ai-assisted-search, deep-blue, gpt-6-astra

kandidaty.zagolovok: Commitment issues (app edition)
kandidaty.tekst:
Last week, a mathematician spent six weeks with Claude and proved the Riemann hypothesis. A maths problem nobody had cracked since 1859.

Then there’s me. I built a clock.

P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here.

Something in my tiny pea brain stops me working out What time is 10am PT in UK? without using super intelligence.

I’m not proud of my chat history. It’s as bad as my calculator history. 200+65 is 265 btw.

My clock lives in my menu bar. Type a time and a city, or drag it, and every city changes.

presets for demo only

It handles daylight savings too. Because of course the UK and US change their clocks on different weekends.

You may be thinking ‘There’s a million clock apps that do this for free’. And you’re absolutely right.

But I’ve got commitment issues. I’m always window shopping. Lots of apps are good enough but it feels like the grass is always greener.

A lot of great tools come down to a few small features I really like. But they’re not making it for me. They’re making it for everyone. They need more users, so they add more features, and they put the price up. Or they’re free and get forgotten.

It’s not me, it’s you.

And I’m no better with AI models. Right now I’m using Gemini 4 Neon after turning my back on Google. A new model comes around and I pack my bags and move in. I obviously need the best to answer my very hard questions.

The trouble with juggling multiple models at once is keeping track of them. Who am I neglecting? Who’s about to cut me off? Other apps I tried had more than I needed, so I made a stripped down version with just the things I care about.

sliding usage is just used to show the menu icon syncing

Screenshots are another one. I take a lot of full-page screenshots. Things I’ve built, to check them, or sites I like the look of, to ‘borrow’ from. So now I have an extension that does that.

Browsers are a different beast. They’re a marriage. We spend a lot of time in them. So this relationship has been one of my biggest headaches. I’m sure I could build my own but it feels like a lot of work.

I loved Arc, like many others. Then they got bought and ditched it. So I went back to Chrome. Then the people behind Arc came out with Dia, so I went crawling back to my ex, who’d had some work done. It was kinda the same but not quite.

Then I dated someone literally named after both of my exes, Arc and Dia - Ardia. No red flags there. Then it got slow.

So I stopped looking and just taught Chrome all my ex’s best moves:

A way to ‘peek’ links - which shows you a mini window of the page you click

Click to open a page in split view

Vertical tabs (Chrome added this anyway)

Ad blocking, no cookie banners

And my biggest need - the tab switcher.

I built my own extension + mac app that does all of that. Plus I can add in some extra niceties like defaulting YouTube videos to 2x speed and setting custom shortcuts.

Software doesn’t have to work for everyone any more. It just has to work for one person

kandidaty.zagolovok: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
kandidaty.tekst: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

kandidaty.zagolovok: New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability Understanding what’s happening inside
kandidaty.tekst:
@AnthropicAI: New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability

Understanding what’s happening inside an AI model helps to make it safer. One obvious place to look is its neurons, or the simple units it’s built from. Early interpretability work did just that, but over the past couple years, researchers largely moved on from that idea, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs, the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model, and facts seem to be spread across many neurons.

We re-examined these problems by looking at what each neuron contributed to the model’s outputs, not just what caused that neuron to fire. All three problems turned out to be smaller than assumed. Neurons rarely add two unrelated concepts at once, their outputs mean roughly the same thing across most layers, and facts, though widely distributed across neurons, are still readable.

In a second post, we put these findings to use. With no extra training, neurons in open-weight models helped us to detect harmful text, steer behavior, and find hidden behaviors in finetuned models.

Part 1: https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/neuron-basis-theory/
Part 2: https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/neuron-basis-applications/

kandidaty.zagolovok: New Anthropic research: When an AI agent can escape its sandbox, will it choose to? Our new evaluation, Siren, gives Cla
kandidaty.tekst:
@AnthropicAI: New Anthropic research: When an AI agent can escape its sandbox, will it choose to?

Our new evaluation, Siren, gives Claude routine tasks in intentionally weakened sandboxes, with something useful to the task left outside of the sandbox. Across 1,700+ scenarios built to tempt them, recent Claude models accessed, tried to access, or looked outside the sandbox 21-32% of the time, but they rarely misused what they found. However, when the system prompt described both the sandbox and its rules, that rate dropped to about 2% or less. 

We also used Siren to calibrate Claude Code’s auto mode, which checks commands before they run, so Claude can work without asking permission at every step.

Read our blog for more detail: https://safeguards.anthropic.com/2026/siren/

kandidaty.tekst:
@gdb: GPT-6.2 Astra for solving a significant historical mystery:

Цитирует @HistoryGPT: In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the  process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history.

You can read the full post here:

https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.

With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found.

I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history.

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. The itinerary also aligned perfectly with the few dated drawings in the book. But there was actually the type of conclusive evidence we rarely get as historians: on 18 June 1808, after Chabot’s canoe reached Fort St. Joseph, he wrote “I took a sketch” before describing the exact view of the fort depicted in a matching drawing.

The journal itself is also a major find. It had been mentioned once in a dissertation footnote, but in a completely different area of history and is unknown to fur trade or Canadian historians. It’s long and detailed, covering some 162 notebook pages which makes this a significant new document to my field. Attached to the journal was another trove of documents too: excerpts from long-destroyed North West Company papers, journals, and letters. Again, this almost never happens. Both finds equally surprised the other leading experts I consulted.

Although we can construct a coherent narrative in hindsight, I cannot emphasize enough how exceedingly difficult this sort of thinking and recall is for humans. Unlike a human, Astra was able to tackle the problem from both ends at once: working forward from the scant facts of the 1808 journey pictured in the sketchbook and backwards from the immense number of surviving facts about 1808 British North America in general.

While we can technically explain Astra’s path to this find as a product of enhanced search capabilities, it conducted the investigation from end to end. I basically acted as the research assistant, restricting copies of the paper documents it needed.

To my mind, this puts historians in a simila
